articleTitle: User interface considerations for expert diagnostic systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Based Diagnosis
abstract: Consideration is given to interface requirements for both development and use of expert diagnostic systems. Artificial intelligence (Al) techniques discussed include graphical representations, natural language understanding, English-Like Formalisms, and uncertainty reasoning. The argument is made for increased use of qualitative, as opposed to quantitative, representation of uncertainty in order to enhance user interactions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A real time knowledge based recovery advisor for electrical power distribution networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Based Diagnosis
abstract: A common application of expert systems in industry is in the diagnosis of plant health status from monitored data. This paper describes an application of knowledge based techniques to aid engineers maintain electrical supplies. Such a system has been developed for use by control engineers at a Royal Naval dockyard. In the event of network failure leading to loss of supply to a ship, the system will advise the control engineer on the most desirable reconfiguration of the network which restores power to the affected boat(s). The aim of the system is to produce an electrical lineup similar to that which would be proposed by a practising control engineer. The system therefore encompasses some of the engineers 'rules of thumb', as well as obeying obvious electrical constraints. The system has three principle elements; a monitor, a recovery advisor and a network simulator, each is briefly described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Evaluation of a statistical diagnostic system (GLADYS)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Based Diagnosis
abstract: A long term collaborative programme has led to the development and testing of a computer based decision aid to improve management and diagnosis of a common problem in medical practice, namely nonacute gastro-intestinal symptoms to which the authors apply the broad term dyspepsia. The steps in this work are outlined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Diagnostic support in the Oxford System of Medicine
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Based Diagnosis
abstract: The Oxford System of Medicine (OSM) project was started in 1985 with the aim of producing a working specification for a decision support system for general practitioners. The feasibility of such a project seems to depend upon designing a system that is acceptable to general practitioners and acquiring, verifying and maintaining the knowledge base. The authors consider that a knowledge-based theory of decision making, coupled to strategic and policy defining knowledge about diagnosis or any other task, and separated from the simple facts of medicine could be the cornerstone for a decision support system that is flexible enough to provide a suitable environment for author, editor and general practitioner. They present an example of diagnostic consultation starting with the problem of a swelling joint.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Based Diagnosis
abstract: In order to provide an overview of computer based medical diagnosis the author sets out the major theoretical commitments involved. First he presents the AI problem solving paradigm, then the use of decision trees to map symptoms into diseases, next the need to apply Bayes theorem since symptoms are noisy and unreliable and the difficulties with doing so. The role of hypothesis and test and weak model of the causal processes is discussed (stronger models are difficult to use). He then notes the success of second generation expert systems in providing explicit representation of strategic reasoning and a structural representation of domain knowledge. Finally he concludes by describing the unifying capability of the second generation expert systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Based Diagnosis
abstract: The author gives an example of how to write a simple parallel program and explains the significance of the communications overhead. This leads to the idea of course grain and fine grain implementation. The author then explains the point-to-point communications system, called link in the Inmos Transputer, for sending data between programs and the four links per processor limit of the Transputer. Another method of sending data is by sharing memory between processor. The author's department intends to build a computer based on the T800 Transputer but with a distributed memory architecture. The implementation (which will use a Unix like operating system from Perihelion Software) should be efficient for expert systems and large databases.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Coping with uncertainty (in medical diagnostic computing)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Computer Based Diagnosis
abstract: A number of different kinds of uncertainty need to be faced in computer-aided diagnosis. For example, there may be both qualitative and quantitative doubts concerning the background knowledge, and data on a patient may be fragmentary or of dubious quality. The author describes a methodology intended to handle both the propagation of evidence through the network as data on a new case is obtained, and to allow monitoring, criticism and adaptation of both quantitative and qualitative aspects of the model as the database accumulates.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
